In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Just Say No to Single Embeddings: Why Your AI Needs Multiple Perspectives
papers.research_question: How does BERT represent linguistic features internally, and what is the geometric structure of these representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT represents linguistic features in separate semantic and syntactic subspaces, provides evidence of fine-grained geometric representation of word senses, and gives a mathematical argument for the squared-distance tree embedding.
papers.conclusion: The paper's experiments suggest that BERT's internal geometry consists of multiple linear subspaces for different syntactic and semantic information, and that understanding this geometry can help improve transformer architectures.
papers.key_findings:
Attention matrices encode syntactic dependency relations, as shown by linear probes achieving high accuracy.
Parse tree embeddings in BERT approximate Pythagorean embeddings (squared Euclidean distance corresponds to tree distance), and there is a mathematical justification for this.
Word senses are represented as clusters in embedding space, and a simple nearest-neighbor classifier on BERT embeddings achieves state-of-the-art word sense disambiguation.
Semantic information can be isolated in a lower-dimensional subspace via a learned linear transformation (semantic probe).
Concatenating sentences with different word senses can cause embeddings to shift towards the opposing sense, indicating that tokens absorb meaning from all neighboring tokens.
future_direction: Investigating other meaningful subspaces in BERT's internal geometry
Using internal geometry to improve or refine transformer architectures
papers.abstract: Note: This is a work in progress document We present empirical evidence that conversations exhibit consistent geometric signatures when projected into different embedding spaces, alongside surprising variability in local feature detection. Analyzing 229 multi-agent AI dialogues from our prior study on social dynamics [Garcia, 2025], we examine whether geometric properties of conversational trajectories remain consistent across 5 fundamentally different embedding models. Our analysis reveals a striking dichotomy: while global geometric patterns (distance matrices, trajectory shapes) show remarkable consistency across both transformer-based and classical embeddings (correlations ranging from 0.521 to 0.957), local phase detection exhibits extreme variability (F1 scores from 0.08 to 0.36, agreement correlations from -0.14 to 0.76). This pattern of high global consistency with low local agreement suggests that different embedding models may capture distinct projections of conversations existing in a higher-dimensional semantic space. Transport-based analysis supports this interpretation, showing threefold increases in cross-paradigm distances compared to within-paradigm distances. These findings establish that while geometric analysis of conversation captures genuine structural properties, the global-local dichotomy implies fundamental limits on fine-grained analysis and raises intriguing questions about the true dimensionality of conversational dynamics.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Interpreting and improving natural-language processing (in machines) with natural language-processing (in the brain)
papers.research_question: How can brain activity recordings be used to interpret neural network representations, and can aligning models with brain activity improve their language understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a method to interpret neural network representations by aligning them with brain activity recordings, and shows that increasing brain-alignment in BERT improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Aligning NLP models with brain activity can provide insights into their representations and lead to improved language understanding, as demonstrated by improved syntactic performance of brain-altered BERT.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers of transformers are better at predicting brain activity for longer contexts.
Transformer-XL's performance does not degrade with longer context, unlike other models.
Uniform attention in shallow layers of BERT improves brain activity prediction for contexts up to 25 words.
Altering BERT to have uniform attention in shallow layers improves its performance on syntactic tasks.
Different models (ELMo, USE, BERT, Transformer-XL) encode context information differently.
papers.limitation:
Reverse inference in brain imaging can lead to erroneous conclusions because a brain region can be involved in more than one task.
Direct comparison of performance between different networks is misleading because information is likely organized differently across networks.
papers.abstract: Neural networks models for NLP are typically implemented without the explicit encoding of language rules and yet they are able to break one performance record after another. This has generated a lot of research interest in interpreting the representations learned by these networks. We propose here a novel interpretation approach that relies on the only processing system we have that does understand language: the human brain. We use brain imaging recordings of subjects reading complex natural text to interpret word and sequence embeddings from 4 recent NLP models - ELMo, USE, BERT and Transformer-XL. We study how their representations differ across layer depth, context length, and attention type. Our results reveal differences in the context-related representations across these models. Further, in the transformer models, we find an interaction between layer depth and context length, and between layer depth and attention type. We finally hypothesize that altering BERT to better align with brain recordings would enable it to also better understand language. Probing the altered BERT using syntactic NLP tasks reveals that the model with increased brain-alignment outperforms the original model. Cognitive neuroscientists have already begun using NLP networks to study the brain, and this work closes the loop to allow the interaction between NLP and cognitive neuroscience to be a true cross-pollination.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of transformer LLMs on compositional tasks, and are their errors incidental or do they signal fundamental limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LLMs solve compositional tasks via linearized subgraph matching rather than systematic reasoning, and they exhibit exponential error accumulation with increased complexity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers have inherent limitations in solving compositionally complex tasks, and fundamental innovations are needed to address these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers' accuracy on compositional tasks drops to near zero as task complexity increases.
Fine-tuning on task-specific data leads to near-perfect in-domain performance but poor out-of-domain generalization.
Transformers learn surface patterns (e.g., via relative information gain) rather than underlying algorithms.
Correct predictions correlate with frequency of subgraph patterns in training data, indicating pattern matching.
Error analysis shows propagation errors dominate, indicating failure to compose steps.
papers.limitation: Due to budget constraints, grokking experiments were only conducted on the multiplication task.
future_direction: Using transformers for tasks decomposable into few reasoning steps
Using transformers in combination with planning modules or refinement methods
Fundamental innovations to address limitations
papers.abstract: Transformer large language models (LLMs) have sparked admiration for their exceptional performance on tasks that demand intricate multi-step reasoning. Yet, these models simultaneously show failures on surprisingly trivial problems. This begs the question: Are these errors incidental, or do they signal more substantial limitations? In an attempt to demystify transformer LLMs, we investigate the limits of these models across three representative compositional tasks -- multi-digit multiplication, logic grid puzzles, and a classic dynamic programming problem. These tasks require breaking problems down into sub-steps and synthesizing these steps into a precise answer. We formulate compositional tasks as computation graphs to systematically quantify the level of complexity, and break down reasoning steps into intermediate sub-procedures. Our empirical findings suggest that transformer LLMs solve compositional tasks by reducing multi-step compositional reasoning into linearized subgraph matching, without necessarily developing systematic problem-solving skills. To round off our empirical study, we provide theoretical arguments on abstract multi-step reasoning problems that highlight how autoregressive generations' performance can rapidly decay with\,increased\,task\,complexity.

papers.title: Layer-Wise Analysis Reveals Universal Discrete Emergence Across Large Language Model Architectures
papers.research_question: How do capabilities emerge in large language models? Do they emerge abruptly or gradually, at which network depths, and is there a universal ordering of emergence across architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that capability emergence in LLMs is abrupt and follows a universal task hierarchy across diverse architectures, with simpler capabilities emerging in shallower layers and abstract reasoning requiring deeper computation.
papers.conclusion: These findings establish a quantitative framework for understanding neural network capability formation, with implications for safety through predictability, interpretability through mechanistic localization, and architecture design through principled optimization of emergence properties.
papers.key_findings:
Nearly all model-task combinations show abrupt accuracy transitions (discrete phase changes) rather than gradual improvement.
Post-emergence performance converges to consistent levels across conditions, suggesting binary competence states.
There is a robust task-dependent emergence ordering: language understanding emerges earliest, then mathematical reasoning, then commonsense reasoning, and boolean output formatting emerges latest.
This hierarchy is consistent across all tested architectures (Llama, Phi, DeepSeek).
Architectural design and training quality dominate model size in determining emergence timing.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> The mechanisms underlying capability emergence in large language models remain poorly characterized. This study conducts system atic layer-by-layer probing across seven architecturally diverse models spanning three orders of magnitude in size, testing mathematical rea soning, logical inference, commonsense reasoning, and language under standing. Nearly all model task combinations exhibit abrupt accuracy transitions at speci c network depths rather than gradual improve ment, providing strong evidence for discrete phase changes in capabil ity formation. Post-emergence performance converges to remarkably consistent levels across all tested conditions, suggesting binary com petence states in which abilities are either absent or fully expressed. The analysis reveals robust task-dependent emergence ordering, with linguistically simpler capabilities crystallizing in shallower layers while abstract reasoning requires deeper computation. This hierarchy proves consistent across all tested architectures, indicating universal orga nizing principles independent of model family or training procedure. Size-dependent e ects appear complex and non-monotonic, with some larger models exhibiting earlier emergence while others show delayed capability formation, suggesting that architectural details modulate pure scaling e ects. These ndings establish a quantitative framework for understanding neural network capability formation, with implica tions for safety through predictability, interpretability through mech anistic localization, and architecture design through principled opti mization of emergence properties.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Progress measures for grokking via mechanistic interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we find continuous progress measures that underlie seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes (like grokking) in neural networks? The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to reverse-engineer learned behaviors and define such progress measures.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uses mechanistic interpretability to define progress measures for grokking, showing that grokking arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms (a Fourier multiplication algorithm) followed by removal of memorizing components, rather than being a sudden shift.
papers.conclusion: Grokking is not a sudden shift but results from gradual mechanisms, and mechanistic interpretability can reveal progress measures that track the development of emergent behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The transformers implement modular addition using a Fourier multiplication algorithm that maps inputs to a circle and uses trigonometric identities.
The model's weights and activations show periodic structure and are sparse in the Fourier domain, with key frequencies.
Two progress measures (restricted loss and excluded loss) improve continuously prior to grokking, revealing hidden progress.
Training can be split into three phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup.
The sudden transition to perfect test accuracy occurs during cleanup, after the generalizing mechanism is already learned.
papers.limitation: There is significant uncertainty about the scalability of mechanistic interpretability approaches to large models.
future_direction: Apply the approach to more complex tasks and models.
Use progress measures to predict and understand emergent behavior in large language models.
Explore task-independent progress measures.
papers.abstract: Neural networks often exhibit emergent behavior, where qualitatively new capabilities arise from scaling up the amount of parameters, training data, or training steps. One approach to understanding emergence is to find continuous \textit{progress measures} that underlie the seemingly discontinuous qualitative changes. We argue that progress measures can be found via mechanistic interpretability: reverse-engineering learned behaviors into their individual components. As a case study, we investigate the recently-discovered phenomenon of ``grokking'' exhibited by small transformers trained on modular addition tasks. We fully reverse engineer the algorithm learned by these networks, which uses discrete Fourier transforms and trigonometric identities to convert addition to rotation about a circle. We confirm the algorithm by analyzing the activations and weights and by performing ablations in Fourier space. Based on this understanding, we define progress measures that allow us to study the dynamics of training and split training into three continuous phases: memorization, circuit formation, and cleanup. Our results show that grokking, rather than being a sudden shift, arises from the gradual amplification of structured mechanisms encoded in the weights, followed by the later removal of memorizing components.

papers.title: Tracing the complexity profiles of different linguistic phenomena through the intrinsic dimension of LLM representations
papers.research_question: Does the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations serve as a marker for linguistic complexity, and can it differentiate between formal and functional complexity?
papers.core_contribution: The intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations is a useful marker for linguistic complexity, allowing differentiation between formal and functional complexity, and points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity in LLMs, it allows differentiation between formal and functional complexity, and it points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
ID profiles differentiate between formal complexity (coordination vs. subordination) and functional complexity (right-branching vs. center-embedding, unambiguous vs. ambiguous).
The formal complexity contrast emerges in layers coinciding with the generic ID peak, a phase of deep linguistic processing.
Functional complexity contrasts are also reflected in ID but in a less marked way and not correlated with the same processing phase.
Representational similarity (Information Imbalance) and ablation experiments confirm these trends.
Different LLMs show consistent ID profiles and processing stages.
papers.limitation:
Due to compute restrictions, experiments cannot be extended to larger language models.
Results should be reproduced in languages other than English and with more naturalistic data.
A clear mechanistic explanation of the relation between intrinsic dimension and the linguistic phenomena is needed.
future_direction: Ascertain the extent to which observed patterns depend on model size and their emergence during training.
Reproduce results in languages other than English and with more naturalistic data.
Establish a clear mechanistic explanation of the relation between intrinsic dimension and linguistic phenomena.
papers.abstract: We explore the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations as a marker of linguistic complexity, asking if different ID profiles across LLM layers differentially characterize formal and functional complexity. We find the formal contrast between sentences with multiple coordinated or subordinated clauses to be reflected in ID differences whose onset aligns with a phase of more abstract linguistic processing independently identified in earlier work. The functional contrasts between sentences characterized by right branching vs. center embedding or unambiguous vs. ambiguous relative clause attachment are also picked up by ID, but in a less marked way, and they do not correlate with the same processing phase. Further experiments using representational similarity and layer ablation confirm the same trends. We conclude that ID is a useful marker of linguistic complexity in LLMs, that it allows to differentiate between different types of complexity, and that it points to similar stages of linguistic processing across disparate LLMs.

papers.title: How Syntax Specialization Emerges in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does syntactic specialization emerge and evolve over training, and how do model initialization, scale, and training data shape this development?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Syntactic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure syntactic specialization in language models, revealing that syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, exhibits a critical period, and is consistent across architectures but implemented by different neurons.
papers.conclusion: Provides the first systematic, mechanistic account of how syntactic specialization emerges in transformer language models by introducing SSI and applying it across training trajectories, seeds, and model scales, offering an integrated picture of when, where, and how syntax is represented.
papers.key_findings:
SSI correlates with grammaticality judgment accuracy and outperforms supervised probing methods like SVM and regression.
Syntactic specialization emerges gradually during training, with different syntactic phenomena showing distinct acquisition timelines and layer profiles.
There is a critical period (around 16 million tokens) during which syntactic specialization rapidly emerges and then stabilizes.
While layer-level syntactic representations converge across different random seeds, the specific neurons responsible for syntax sensitivity differ (convergent layers, divergent neurons).
Larger models and more training data enhance syntactic abstraction and specialization, but the effect varies across syntactic phenomena.
papers.limitation:
Relies on sentence embeddings (mean pooling) which may miss token-level nuance or positional dynamics.
BLiMP focuses on binary acceptability, leaving gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures underexplored.
Open theoretical questions about minimal inductive bias, architectural interventions, and relation to semantic grounding.
future_direction: Extend SSI to token-level activations or attention maps.
Explore gradient judgments, semantic-pragmatic interactions, and multi-sentence structures beyond binary acceptability.
Investigate the minimal inductive bias or data regime required for syntactic specialization, architectural interventions, and how syntactic development relates to semantic grounding.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been found to develop surprising internal specializations: Individual neurons, attention heads, and circuits become selectively sensitive to syntactic structure, reflecting patterns observed in the human brain. While this specialization is well-documented, how it emerges during training and what influences its development remains largely unknown. In this work, we tap into the black box of specialization by tracking its formation over time. By quantifying internal syntactic consistency across minimal pairs from various syntactic phenomena, we identify a clear developmental trajectory: Syntactic sensitivity emerges gradually, concentrates in specific layers, and exhibits a 'critical period' of rapid internal specialization. This process is consistent across architectures and initialization parameters (e.g., random seeds), and is influenced by model scale and training data. We therefore reveal not only where syntax arises in LLMs but also how some models internalize it during training. To support future research, we will release the code, models, and training checkpoints upon acceptance.

papers.title: Contextual Feature Extraction Hierarchies Converge in Large Language Models and the Brain
papers.research_question: What factors contribute to the alignment of large language models (LLMs) with the brain's language processing mechanisms, and do LLMs share fundamental computational principles that increasingly align with the spoken language processing pathway in the human brain?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that higher-performing large language models (LLMs) exhibit greater alignment with the brain's hierarchical language processing, and that contextual information is a key factor driving this convergence.
papers.conclusion: The findings reveal that hierarchical structure and contextual dependencies are fundamental to language processing, leading to convergent strategies in both artificial and biological systems.
papers.key_findings:
Higher-performing LLMs achieve higher peak brain similarity scores.
Better-performing LLMs peak in brain similarity at earlier layers compared to lower-performing models.
Better-performing LLMs have hierarchical feature extraction pathways that more closely align with the brain's hierarchy.
Contextual information is crucial for brain similarity and hierarchy alignment, with long context windows being particularly important.
Top-performing LLMs converge in their feature extraction hierarchies, as shown by high inter-model similarity.
papers.limitation:
Limited iEEG coverage may not capture all relevant brain regions.
The speech comprehension task is simple and may not fully engage higher-level language processing.
LLMs are trained for next-word prediction, which differs from the comprehension task performed by subjects.
future_direction: Using brain similarity as an evaluation metric for LLM development.
Improving contextual processing in LLMs to enhance performance and brain alignment.
Investigating the role of later layers in LLMs for higher-order integration.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in artificial intelligence have sparked interest in the parallels between large language models (LLMs) and human neural processing, particularly in language comprehension. While prior research has established similarities in the representation of LLMs and the brain, the underlying computational principles that cause this convergence, especially in the context of evolving LLMs, remain elusive. Here, we examined a diverse selection of high-performance LLMs with similar parameter sizes to investigate the factors contributing to their alignment with the brain's language processing mechanisms. We find that as LLMs achieve higher performance on benchmark tasks, they not only become more brain-like as measured by higher performance when predicting neural responses from LLM embeddings, but also their hierarchical feature extraction pathways map more closely onto the brain's while using fewer layers to do the same encoding. We also compare the feature extraction pathways of the LLMs to each other and identify new ways in which high-performing models have converged toward similar hierarchical processing mechanisms. Finally, we show the importance of contextual information in improving model performance and brain similarity. Our findings reveal the converging aspects of language processing in the brain and LLMs and offer new directions for developing models that align more closely with human cognitive processing.

papers.title: Do Vision Transformers See Like Convolutional Neural Networks?
papers.research_question: How are Vision Transformers solving image tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds key representational differences between Vision Transformers (ViTs) and Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), showing ViTs have more uniform layer representations, incorporate global information earlier via self-attention, and have stronger skip connections that propagate features differently.
papers.conclusion: ViTs and CNNs have clear differences in features and internal structure, with ViTs using global features early and strong skip connections, while local information aggregation is learned from scratch at scale. ViTs show strong spatial localization, promising for future uses like object detection.
papers.key_findings:
ViTs have a more uniform internal representation structure with greater similarity between lower and higher layers compared to the staged similarity in ResNets.
ViTs incorporate global information in lower layers through self-attention, while CNNs are restricted to local receptive fields; this leads to quantitatively different features.
Skip connections in ViTs are more influential than in ResNets, with a phase transition: early layers strongly propagate the CLS token, while later layers propagate spatial token representations.
ViTs preserve input spatial information more faithfully than ResNets in higher layers, especially when trained with a CLS token rather than global average pooling.
Large-scale pretraining data is crucial for ViTs to learn to attend locally in early layers and to develop high-quality intermediate representations for transfer learning.
papers.limitation: The study uses CKA, which summarizes measurements into a single scalar; while complemented with interventional tests and linear probes, more fine-grained methods may reveal additional insights.
papers.abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have so far been the de-facto model for visual data. Recent work has shown that (Vision) Transformer models (ViT) can achieve comparable or even superior performance on image classification tasks. This raises a central question: how are Vision Transformers solving these tasks? Are they acting like convolutional networks, or learning entirely different visual representations? Analyzing the internal representation structure of ViTs and CNNs on image classification benchmarks, we find striking differences between the two architectures, such as ViT having more uniform representations across all layers. We explore how these differences arise, finding crucial roles played by self-attention, which enables early aggregation of global information, and ViT residual connections, which strongly propagate features from lower to higher layers. We study the ramifications for spatial localization, demonstrating ViTs successfully preserve input spatial information, with noticeable effects from different classification methods. Finally, we study the effect of (pretraining) dataset scale on intermediate features and transfer learning, and conclude with a discussion on connections to new architectures such as the MLP-Mixer.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Toward Mechanistic Explanation of Deductive Reasoning in Language Models
papers.research_question: How does a small language model solve a deductive reasoning task, and what internal mechanisms (e.g., induction heads) are involved in implementing the logical inference?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a small language model can learn deductive reasoning by implementing rule-based circuits, with induction heads playing a central role, and introduces a truncated pseudoinverse technique for decoding query, key, and value information.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that a tiny LM can learn deductive reasoning by implementing symbolic rule-based circuits, with induction heads being a fundamental component, and suggests that induction heads may also be central in more complex logical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A simplified NanoGPT model trained with Chain-of-Thought can learn deductive reasoning rules and generalize to unseen examples.
Induction heads are crucial for implementing rule completion and rule chaining steps in the logical inference.
The model learns the underlying inference rules rather than memorizing patterns.
A single attention head can host multiple induction heads and other circuits, simplifying post-hoc explanation.
Training without Chain-of-Thought leads to memorization and poor generalization, indicating the importance of CoT for learning rules.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability techniques used (e.g., residual stream decoding and truncated pseudoinverse) are not 100% precise and may fail to decode the expected tokens.
The deductive reasoning task is simple and does not reflect the complexity of real-world logical reasoning.
future_direction: Investigating whether one-layer circuits resembling induction heads can be created by modifying the attention mechanism to decouple key and value positions.
Exploring the role of induction heads in solving more complex logical problems with larger language models.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have demonstrated relevant capabilities in solving problems that require logical reasoning; however, the corresponding internal mechanisms remain largely unexplored. In this paper, we show that a small language model can solve a deductive reasoning task by learning the underlying rules (rather than operating as a statistical learner). A low-level explanation of its internal representations and computational circuits is then provided. Our findings reveal that induction heads play a central role in the implementation of the rule completion and rule chaining steps involved in the logical inference required by the task.

papers.title: Linguistic generalization and compositionality in modern artificial neural networks
papers.research_question: How do modern deep artificial neural networks achieve linguistic generalization and productivity, and do they rely on systematic compositional rules?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reviews evidence that modern deep neural networks can achieve sophisticated linguistic generalization without relying on systematic compositional rules, and argues this behavior offers a new perspective on computational strategies for linguistic productivity relevant to cognitive science.
papers.conclusion: Modern deep neural networks are proficient at language processing and exhibit subtle grammatical generalization, yet they do not rely on systematic compositional rules, offering a comparative perspective for studying linguistic productivity and non-systematic generalization patterns in human language.
papers.key_findings:
Neural networks can capture abstract, structure-dependent grammatical generalizations (e.g., long-distance number agreement) even in nonsensical sentences.
These networks fail at systematic compositional generalization in controlled tasks like the SCAN benchmark (e.g., jump and around-right splits).
Some architectures (e.g., convolutional seq2seq) show partial success on compositional splits but without systematicity, making errors uniformly across composition frames.
In communication games, neural networks can develop productive but non-compositional codes that generalize as well as compositional ones.
Analysis of a network's internal circuitry (e.g., ablation studies) suggests it develops genuine grammatical processing mechanisms rather than relying on surface heuristics.
papers.limitation: Our current understanding of the strategies learned by these networks is very limited, and better analytical tools are needed to uncover the mechanisms behind the dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.
future_direction: Develop better analytical tools to uncover the mechanisms that lead to the detected dissociation of productive grammatical competence and systematic compositionality.

Investigate whether making neural networks more compositional, for example by means of more structured modular architectures, will make them more adaptive and faster at learning without sacrificing generality.

Use progress in understanding the linguistic capabilities of neural networks to make precise predictions about the origin, scope, and mechanics of non-systematic productive phenomena in human language.
papers.abstract: In the last decade, deep artificial neural networks have achieved astounding performance in many natural language-processing tasks. Given the high productivity of language, these models must possess effective generalization abilities. It is widely assumed that humans handle linguistic productivity by means of algebraic compositional rules: are deep networks similarly compositional? After reviewing the main innovations characterizing current deep language-processing networks, I discuss a set of studies suggesting that deep networks are capable of subtle grammar-dependent generalizations, but also that they do not rely on systematic compositional rules. I argue that the intriguing behaviour of these devices (still awaiting a full understanding) should be of interest to linguists and cognitive scientists, as it offers a new perspective on possible computational strategies to deal with linguistic productivity beyond rule-based compositionality, and it might lead to new insights into the less systematic generalization patterns that also appear in natural language. This article is part of the theme issue 'Towards mechanistic models of meaning composition'.

papers.title: Humanlike Cognitive Patterns as Emergent Phenomena in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models exhibit human-like cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a comprehensive review of LLMs' emergent cognitive patterns in decision-making, reasoning, and creativity, comparing them to human benchmarks and highlighting partial alignment, advancements in advanced models, and potential for collaboration.
papers.conclusion: The review synthesizes evidence that LLMs partially replicate human cognitive patterns, with notable advancements in reasoning and creativity, but limitations remain, indicating the need for further research in memory, attention, and open-source model development.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate several human-like decision-making biases but lack others such as reflection effect and waste aversion.
Advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short.
LLMs show strong analogical reasoning abilities, sometimes surpassing human performance.
In creativity, LLMs excel in language-based tasks but struggle with divergent thinking requiring real-world context.
LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators to augment human creativity in problem-solving settings.
papers.limitation:
Over-reliance on GPT family models and insufficient testing of open-source LLMs, leading to potential bias and non-replication.
Memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs have not been sufficiently studied compared to decision-making, reasoning, and creativity.
future_direction: Study memory and attention mechanisms in LLMs
Increase testing and use of open-source LLMs
Adopt practices using multiple models in experiments
papers.abstract: Research on emergent patterns in Large Language Models (LLMs) has gained significant traction in both psychology and artificial intelligence, motivating the need for a comprehensive review that offers a synthesis of this complex landscape. In this article, we systematically review LLMs' capabilities across three important cognitive domains: decision-making biases, reasoning, and creativity. We use empirical studies drawing on established psychological tests and compare LLMs' performance to human benchmarks. On decision-making, our synthesis reveals that while LLMs demonstrate several human-like biases, some biases observed in humans are absent, indicating cognitive patterns that only partially align with human decision-making. On reasoning, advanced LLMs like GPT-4 exhibit deliberative reasoning akin to human System-2 thinking, while smaller models fall short of human-level performance. A distinct dichotomy emerges in creativity: while LLMs excel in language-based creative tasks, such as storytelling, they struggle with divergent thinking tasks that require real-world context. Nonetheless, studies suggest that LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators, augmenting creativity in human-machine problem-solving settings. Discussing key limitations, we also offer guidance for future research in areas such as memory, attention, and open-source model development.

papers.title: What Does BERT Look at? An Analysis of BERT’s Attention
papers.research_question: What specific linguistic features does BERT learn from unlabeled data, as revealed by its attention mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that BERT's attention heads capture syntactic and coreference information, and proposes methods for analyzing attention mechanisms to reveal this linguistic knowledge.
papers.conclusion: Attention maps contain substantial linguistic knowledge and complement other model analysis techniques, and should be part of the toolkit for understanding what neural networks learn about language.
papers.key_findings:
BERT's attention heads exhibit common patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence.
Certain attention heads specialize to specific syntactic relations (e.g., direct objects, determiners) with high accuracy.
One attention head performs well at coreference resolution.
An attention-based probing classifier achieves 77 UAS on dependency parsing, showing BERT's attention captures substantial syntactic information.
Attention heads in the same layer tend to behave similarly.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained neural networks such as BERT have had great recent success in NLP, motivating a growing body of research investigating what aspects of language they are able to learn from unlabeled data. Most recent analysis has focused on model outputs (e.g., language model surprisal) or internal vector representations (e.g., probing classifiers). Complementary to these works, we propose methods for analyzing the attention mechanisms of pre-trained models and apply them to BERT. BERT's attention heads exhibit patterns such as attending to delimiter tokens, specific positional offsets, or broadly attending over the whole sentence, with heads in the same layer often exhibiting similar behaviors. We further show that certain attention heads correspond well to linguistic notions of syntax and coreference. For example, we find heads that attend to the direct objects of verbs, determiners of nouns, objects of prepositions, and coreferent mentions with remarkably high accuracy. Lastly, we propose an attention-based probing classifier and use it to further demonstrate that substantial syntactic information is captured in BERT's attention.

papers.title: Birth of a Transformer: A Memory Viewpoint
papers.research_question: How do transformers balance global knowledge and in-context learning during training, specifically in the development of induction head mechanisms?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a synthetic bigram dataset and an associative memory viewpoint to study learning dynamics in two-layer transformers, showing that induction heads emerge through top-down gradient-based learning.
papers.conclusion: The associative memory viewpoint provides valuable insights into transformer learning dynamics, offering a foundation for better interpretability and improvements in large language models.
papers.key_findings:
Global bigram associations are learned rapidly, while in-context induction mechanisms develop more slowly.
Transformer weight matrices can be viewed as associative memories that store input-output embedding pairs.
The induction head mechanism forms in a top-down manner, with output matrices learning before key-query matrices.
Theoretical gradient analysis shows how associative memories are recovered from noisy inputs during training.
Data distribution properties, such as trigger frequency and output uniformity, affect the learning speed and accuracy of associative memories.
papers.limitation:
The simplified transformer architecture lacks components like non-linear MLPs, multiple heads, and layer normalization, which are present in standard transformers.
The synthetic dataset may not fully capture the complexity of real-world language data.
future_direction: Extending the associative memory viewpoint to non-linear components and multi-head architectures.
Applying insights to optimization algorithms, data selection, and model editing for LLMs.
Studying how such mechanisms scale to larger models and more complex tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models based on transformers have achieved great empirical successes. However, as they are deployed more widely, there is a growing need to better understand their internal mechanisms in order to make them more reliable. These models appear to store vast amounts of knowledge from their training data, and to adapt quickly to new information provided in their context or prompt. We study how transformers balance these two types of knowledge by considering a synthetic setup where tokens are generated from either global or context-specific bigram distributions. By a careful empirical analysis of the training process on a simplified two-layer transformer, we illustrate the fast learning of global bigrams and the slower development of an "induction head" mechanism for the in-context bigrams. We highlight the role of weight matrices as associative memories, provide theoretical insights on how gradients enable their learning during training, and study the role of data-distributional properties.

papers.title: On Identifiability in Transformers
papers.research_question: What is the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings in Transformers, and how does context aggregate into hidden tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention weights are not identifiable and thus not directly interpretable; effective attention and hidden token attribution are proposed as tools to better understand transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention distributions are not directly interpretable due to non-identifiability; effective attention and hidden token attribution are useful tools for understanding transformers, and the relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Attention weights are not identifiable for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, meaning there are infinitely many attention weights yielding the same output.
Effective attention, which removes the null space component, can diverge from raw attention and provide more reliable explanations.
Contextual word embeddings retain their identity (input token) to a large degree across layers, with identity information encoded in the angle.
Input tokens mix strongly in hidden embeddings, with the contribution of the original token decreasing monotonically with depth but remaining the largest individual contributor in most cases.
Context aggregated into hidden embeddings is mostly local, with long-range dependencies increasing in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Effective attention is not guaranteed to be a probability distribution and may have negative weights.
The relationship between token mixing and identifiability warrants further investigation.
future_direction: Further research to understand effective attention and its variants.
Applying the concepts to compare different transformer variants.
papers.abstract: In this paper we delve deep in the Transformer architecture by investigating two of its core components: self-attention and contextual embeddings. In particular, we study the identifiability of attention weights and token embeddings, and the aggregation of context into hidden tokens. We show that, for sequences longer than the attention head dimension, attention weights are not identifiable. We propose effective attention as a complementary tool for improving explanatory interpretations based on attention. Furthermore, we show that input tokens retain to a large degree their identity across the model. We also find evidence suggesting that identity information is mainly encoded in the angle of the embeddings and gradually decreases with depth. Finally, we demonstrate strong mixing of input information in the generation of contextual embeddings by means of a novel quantification method based on gradient attribution. Overall, we show that self-attention distributions are not directly interpretable and present tools to better understand and further investigate Transformer models.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning Enhances Existing Mechanisms: A Case Study on Entity Tracking
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the internal mechanisms for entity tracking in language models? Specifically, does fine-tuning change the circuit for entity tracking, how does the circuit work, and what specific sub-mechanism is improved?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them; the same entity tracking circuit is present and functional in both base and fine-tuned models, with performance gains due to improved handling of positional information.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning enhances existing mechanisms rather than fundamentally altering them.
papers.key_findings:
The same entity tracking circuit is present in both base and fine-tuned models.
The circuit functionality remains the same: entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity.
Performance improvement in fine-tuned models is primarily due to improved handling of augmented positional information.
The circuit in fine-tuned models is larger (superset of the base circuit) but the core mechanism is the same.
Cross-model activation patching (CMAP) can localize the improved sub-mechanism.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to a single task (entity tracking) and a few models (Llama-7B and its fine-tuned variants).
future_direction: Extend the study to more tasks and models.
Investigate whether the enhancement of existing mechanisms is a general principle.
papers.abstract: Fine-tuning on generalized tasks such as instruction following, code generation, and mathematics has been shown to enhance language models' performance on a range of tasks. Nevertheless, explanations of how such fine-tuning influences the internal computations in these models remain elusive. We study how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms implemented in language models. As a case study, we explore the property of entity tracking, a crucial facet of language comprehension, where models fine-tuned on mathematics have substantial performance gains. We identify the mechanism that enables entity tracking and show that (i) in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions primarily the same circuit implements entity tracking. In fact, the entity tracking circuit of the original model on the fine-tuned versions performs better than the full original model. (ii) The circuits of all the models implement roughly the same functionality: Entity tracking is performed by tracking the position of the correct entity in both the original model and its fine-tuned versions. (iii) Performance boost in the fine-tuned models is primarily attributed to its improved ability to handle the augmented positional information. To uncover these findings, we employ: Patch Patching, DCM, which automatically detects model components responsible for specific semantics, and CMAP, a new approach for patching activations across models to reveal improved mechanisms. Our findings suggest that fine-tuning enhances, rather than fundamentally alters, the mechanistic operation of the model.

papers.title: Cognitive Foundations for Reasoning and Their Manifestation in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive elements of reasoning manifest in LLMs, and how do they differ from human reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements for reasoning and conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of human and LLM reasoning traces, revealing that LLMs underutilize cognitive elements correlated with success and that test-time reasoning guidance can improve performance.
papers.conclusion: The taxonomy provides a shared vocabulary for diagnosing reasoning failures and enables principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms, while models possess latent capabilities that can be elicited with structural guidance.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs underutilize cognitive elements that are correlated with success, especially on ill-structured problems.
Humans use more abstraction and conceptual processing, while LLMs rely on surface-level enumeration.
Test-time reasoning guidance that scaffolds successful cognitive structures improves performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems.
The research community focuses on easily quantifiable cognitive elements (like sequential organization) and neglects meta-cognitive controls (like self-awareness).
Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously.
papers.limitation:
Human participants are educated adults; comparison with children might yield different insights.
Models are tested on a limited set of problem types.
future_direction: Using the taxonomy for training and evaluation of LLMs
Developing cognitive architectures based on the taxonomy
Extending the analysis to more problem types and models
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) solve complex problems yet fail on simpler variants, suggesting they achieve correct outputs through mechanisms fundamentally different from human reasoning. To understand this gap, we synthesize cognitive science research into a taxonomy of 28 cognitive elements spanning reasoning invariants, meta-cognitive controls, representations for organizing reasoning & knowledge, and transformation operations. We introduce a fine-grained evaluation framework and conduct the first large-scale empirical analysis of 192K traces from 18 models across text, vision, and audio, complemented by 54 human think-aloud traces, which we make publicly available. We find that models under-utilize cognitive elements correlated with success, narrowing to rigid sequential processing on ill-structured problems where diverse representations and meta-cognitive monitoring are critical. Human traces show more abstraction and conceptual processing, while models default to surface-level enumeration. Meta-analysis of 1.6K LLM reasoning papers reveals the research community concentrates on easily quantifiable elements (sequential organization: 55%, decomposition: 60%) but neglecting meta-cognitive controls (self-awareness: 16%) that correlate with success. Models possess behavioral repertoires associated with success but fail to deploy them spontaneously. Leveraging these patterns, we develop test-time reasoning guidance that automatically scaffold successful structures, improving performance by up to 66.7% on complex problems. By establishing a shared vocabulary between cognitive science and LLM research, our framework enables systematic diagnosis of reasoning failures and principled development of models that reason through robust cognitive mechanisms rather than spurious shortcuts, while providing tools to test theories of human cognition at scale.

papers.title: How to Plant Trees in Language Models: Data and Architectural Effects on the Emergence of Syntactic Inductive Biases
papers.research_question: What architectural features and pre-training data properties contribute to the emergence of hierarchical syntactic inductive biases in language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that model depth is more critical than width for hierarchical syntactic generalization in Transformers, and that pre-training on simpler language like child-directed speech induces such biases with orders-of-magnitude less data than web text.
papers.conclusion: The study finds that model depth is more important than other architectural components for hierarchical generalization, and that simpler pre-training data leads to faster acquisition of syntactic inductive biases, suggesting Transformers may be more data-efficient in cognitively plausible settings.
papers.key_findings:
Model depth has a greater impact on hierarchical generalization than model width or number of parameters alone.
Pre-training on child-directed speech enables hierarchical generalization with far less data (5M words) compared to Wikipedia or web text (100M-1B words).
The number of parameters does not monotonically predict syntactic generalization accuracy.
Syntactic generalization accuracy correlates with language modeling performance and downstream task performance.
Simpler language, such as Simple Wikipedia, also induces hierarchical biases more efficiently than standard Wikipedia.
papers.limitation:
Findings may not generalize to other types of encoder-decoder models, encoder-only, or decoder-only models.
Analysis is based only on English and two syntactic transformations, which may not cover all linguistic phenomena.
future_direction: Using methods to measure the tree-likeness of Transformer representations during pre-training.
Disentangling the effects of lexical and syntactic complexity in pre-training data.
Exploring a two-phase 'starting small' pre-training approach.
papers.abstract: Accurate syntactic representations are essential for robust generalization in natural language. Recent work has found that pre-training can teach language models to rely on hierarchical syntactic features - as opposed to incorrect linear features - when performing tasks after fine-tuning. We test what aspects of pre-training are important for endowing encoder-decoder Transformers with an inductive bias that favors hierarchical syntactic generalizations. We focus on architectural features (depth, width, and number of parameters), as well as the genre and size of the pre-training corpus, diagnosing inductive biases using two syntactic transformation tasks: question formation and passivization, both in English. We find that the number of parameters alone does not explain hierarchical generalization: model depth plays greater role than model width. We also find that pre-training on simpler language, such as child-directed speech, induces a hierarchical bias using an order-of-magnitude less data than pre-training on more typical datasets based on web text or Wikipedia; this suggests that in cognitively plausible language acquisition settings, neural language models may be more data-efficient than previously thought.

papers.title: Word-order Biases in Deep-agent Emergent Communication
papers.research_question: Do sequence-processing neural networks exhibit natural language word-order biases, such as temporal iconicity, avoidance of redundancy, and minimization of long-distance dependencies?
papers.core_contribution: LSTM-based Seq2Seq agents show some natural language word-order biases (like avoiding long-distance dependencies) but not others (like avoiding redundant coding), suggesting the need to incorporate 'effort' to make AI communication more human-like.
papers.conclusion: Seq2Seq agents partially exhibit natural word-order biases, but differ in some aspects (like preference for backward order and weak redundancy avoidance), suggesting incorporating effort-based pressures to make AI communication more human-like.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM agents show a strong tendency to avoid long-distance dependencies.
LSTM agents have a preference for backward-iconic order over forward-iconic, which is opposite to human language.
Only weak tendency towards avoidance of redundant coding (e.g., markers in fixed-order languages).
In iterated learning, free-order languages tend to become more fixed with preferred orders emerging.
Attention-enhanced models learn faster and show some biases more clearly.
future_direction: How to incorporate 'effort'-based pressures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: Sequence-processing neural networks led to remarkable progress on many NLP tasks. As a consequence, there has been increasing interest in understanding to what extent they process language as humans do. We aim here to uncover which biases such models display with respect to "natural" word-order constraints. We train models to communicate about paths in a simple gridworld, using miniature languages that reflect or violate various natural language trends, such as the tendency to avoid redundancy or to minimize long-distance dependencies. We study how the controlled characteristics of our miniature languages affect individual learning and their stability across multiple network generations. The results draw a mixed picture. On the one hand, neural networks show a strong tendency to avoid long-distance dependencies. On the other hand, there is no clear preference for the efficient, non-redundant encoding of information that is widely attested in natural language. We thus suggest inoculating a notion of "effort" into neural networks, as a possible way to make their linguistic behavior more humanlike.

papers.title: Why transformers are obviously good models of language
papers.research_question: Why are transformers effective models of language, and how do they align with theoretical perspectives on language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that transformers are good models of language because their architecture, such as word embeddings and attention mechanisms, aligns with cognitive linguistic theories like prototype theory and construction grammar.
papers.conclusion: Transformers are effective models of language, and their alignment with certain linguistic theories suggests that these theories, such as those from cognitive linguistics, are correct.
papers.key_findings:
Word embeddings in transformers represent prototypical meanings of words, similar to Rosch's prototype theory.
Contextualized word meanings are constructed through self-attention layers, updating prototypes based on context.
Transformers can handle syntax and top-down processing via attention heads and skip connections, analogous to construction grammar.
Transformers lack a bias for local dependencies, allowing them to learn rare long-distance dependencies effectively.
The empirical success of transformers supports cognitive linguistic approaches over traditional syntactic theories.
papers.limitation:
Transformers assert false facts with the same degree of authority as true information.
Transformers have myopia in social contexts, such as not remembering past interactions in chatbots.
papers.abstract: Nobody knows how language works, but many theories abound. Transformers are a class of neural networks that process language automatically with more success than alternatives, both those based on neural computations and those that rely on other (e.g. more symbolic) mechanisms. Here, I highlight direct connections between the transformer architecture and certain theoretical perspectives on language. The empirical success of transformers relative to alternative models provides circumstantial evidence that the linguistic approaches that transformers embody should be, at least, evaluated with greater scrutiny by the linguistics community and, at best, considered to be the currently best available theories.

papers.title: The Rise of Parameter Specialization for Knowledge Storage in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the way knowledge is stored in MLP parameters and the performance of large language models?
papers.core_contribution: Stronger large language models exhibit higher parameter specialization for knowledge storage in MLPs, and this specialization improves the efficiency of knowledge utilization and reduces hallucination.
papers.conclusion: Enhanced parameter specialization for knowledge storage correlates with superior performance in LLMs, and optimizing this specialization improves task performance and reduces hallucination, highlighting the importance of aligning knowledge storage with retrieval mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Stronger models show higher parameter specialization, with PSS correlating strongly with performance on knowledge tasks.
Parameter specialization increases with model scale within the same family.
Parameter specialization evolves during pretraining, increasing in later training steps.
Fine-tuning that enhances parameter specialization (FT-PV) improves performance on knowledge tasks and reduces hallucination compared to other fine-tuning strategies.
Specialized knowledge distribution helps compress knowledge and reduce interference from irrelevant information.
papers.limitation:
Only examined knowledge parameter specialization within the MLP, not attention modules.
Tested models only up to 14B parameters due to GPU limitations.
future_direction: Progressively narrow the focus to individual neurons to measure more precise Parameter Specialization.
Extend the concept to other model architectures like Mixture of Experts (MoE) and Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs).
papers.abstract: Over time, a growing wave of large language models from various series has been introduced to the community. Researchers are striving to maximize the performance of language models with constrained parameter sizes. However, from a microscopic perspective, there has been limited research on how to better store knowledge in model parameters, particularly within MLPs, to enable more effective utilization of this knowledge by the model. In this work, we analyze twenty publicly available open-source large language models to investigate the relationship between their strong performance and the way knowledge is stored in their corresponding MLP parameters. Our findings reveal that as language models become more advanced and demonstrate stronger knowledge capabilities, their parameters exhibit increased specialization. Specifically, parameters in the MLPs tend to be more focused on encoding similar types of knowledge. We experimentally validate that this specialized distribution of knowledge contributes to improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in these models. Furthermore, by conducting causal training experiments, we confirm that this specialized knowledge distribution plays a critical role in improving the model's efficiency in leveraging stored knowledge.

papers.title: Structural Persistence in Language Models: Priming as a Window into Abstract Language Representations
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether modern neural language models exhibit structural priming, what factors influence the priming effect, and the nature of the structural representations they acquire.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer language models exhibit structural priming, indicating they encode abstract structural information, and that this priming is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, with evidence for hierarchical syntactic representations.
papers.conclusion: The study demonstrates that Transformer language models are susceptible to structural priming, revealing they encode abstract structural information that is modulated by semantic and lexical factors, and may involve hierarchical syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer language models show evidence of structural priming.
Priming strength is boosted by semantic similarity and lexical overlap between prime and target sentences.
Priming effects persist but are asymmetrical when primes are semantically implausible.
Priming strength increases with recency (proximity) and cumulative exposure to the prime structure.
The structural representations may encode hierarchical syntactic information, as shown by priming with nested dependencies.
papers.limitation:
The study focuses on only two syntactic alternations in English.
The corpus is template-based and may not capture naturalistic language.
Only auto-regressive language models are considered; masked LMs are not investigated.
future_direction: Extend the investigation to other syntactic constructions and languages.
Use more naturalistic data beyond template-based corpora.
Investigate structural priming in masked language models.
papers.abstract: Abstract We investigate the extent to which modern neural language models are susceptible to structural priming, the phenomenon whereby the structure of a sentence makes the same structure more probable in a follow-up sentence. We explore how priming can be used to study the potential of these models to learn abstract structural information, which is a prerequisite for good performance on tasks that require natural language understanding skills. We introduce a novel metric and release Prime-LM, a large corpus where we control for various linguistic factors that interact with priming strength.
