We find that Transformer models indeed show evidence of structural priming, but also that the generalizations they learned are to some extent modulated by semantic information. Our experiments also show that the representations acquired by the models may not only encode abstract sequential structure but involve certain level of hierarchical syntactic information. More generally, our study shows that the priming paradigm is a useful, additional tool for gaining insights into the capacities of language models and opens the door to future priming-based investigations that probe the model’s internal states.1

papers.title: Examining the Inductive Bias of Neural Language Models with Artificial\n Languages
papers.research_question: What are the inductive biases of neural language models with respect to typological features such as word order, and do these biases reflect tendencies in attested natural languages?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel method using artificial languages to investigate inductive biases of language models in a controlled causal framework, and finds that transformers and LSTMs exhibit different inductive biases regarding word order, with transformers showing clear preferences and LSTMs showing little preference.
papers.conclusion: The paper proposes a novel methodology using carefully controlled artificial languages to study inductive biases, finding that LSTMs and transformers have starkly different inductive biases with respect to word order, with LSTMs showing little variation and transformers showing significant variation across languages.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM-based language models show little preference for any particular word ordering across the artificial languages.
Transformer-based language models show clear preferences for some word orderings over others.
The inductive biases of neither LSTM nor transformer architectures reflect tendencies observed in attested natural languages (e.g., transformers perform similarly on common SOV and rare OVS orders).
The proposed method of using artificial languages allows for controlled causal claims about the effect of typological features on model performance.
Mixed-effects modeling reveals specific interaction effects between typological switches for transformers, but not for LSTMs.
papers.limitation: The artificial grammars are simple and do not cover all possible constructions found in natural languages.
future_direction: Extending the base grammars to test additional hypotheses.
Exploring automated methods for assigning weights to grammar productions.
papers.abstract:
Since language models are used to model a wide variety of languages, it is
natural to ask whether the neural architectures used for the task have
inductive biases towards modeling particular types of languages. Investigation
of these biases has proved complicated due to the many variables that appear in
the experimental setup. Languages vary in many typological dimensions, and it
is difficult to single out one or two to investigate without the others acting
as confounders. We propose a novel method for investigating the inductive
biases of language models using artificial languages. These languages are
constructed to allow us to create parallel corpora across languages that differ
only in the typological feature being investigated, such as word order. We then
use them to train and test language models. This constitutes a fully controlled
causal framework, and demonstrates how grammar engineering can serve as a
useful tool for analyzing neural models. Using this method, we find that
commonly used neural architectures exhibit different inductive biases: LSTMs
display little preference with respect to word ordering, while transformers
display a clear preference for some orderings over others. Further, we find
that neither the inductive bias of the LSTM nor that of the transformer appears
to reflect any tendencies that we see in attested natural languages.

papers.title: Morphosyntactic probing of multilingual BERT models
papers.research_question: To what extent do multilingual masked language models encode morphological information, and where in the context does the disambiguating information reside?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces an extensive multilingual morphological probing dataset and demonstrates that multilingual BERT models effectively encode morphological information, with a tendency for left context to be more informative than right context.
papers.conclusion: Multilingual BERT models encode morphological information effectively, and the asymmetry in context reliance (left over right) is a general property of language, with exceptions tied to typological facts.
papers.key_findings:
mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa achieve strong accuracy on 247 morphological probing tasks across 42 languages, outperforming an LSTM baseline.
XLM-RoBERTa's larger vocabulary makes it better suited for multilingual probing than mBERT.
Preceding context (left context) tends to hold more information for morphological prediction than following context (right context), which is surprising given the non-directional nature of Transformers.
Perturbation effects on probing accuracy correlate with language typological groups.
German is an outlier in the analysis, with different Shapley value distributions compared to other languages.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to 42 languages dominated by Indo-European languages.
papers.abstract: Abstract We introduce an extensive dataset for multilingual probing of morphological information in language models (247 tasks across 42 languages from 10 families), each consisting of a sentence with a target word and a morphological tag as the desired label, derived from the Universal Dependencies treebanks. We find that pre-trained Transformer models (mBERT and XLM-RoBERTa) learn features that attain strong performance across these tasks. We then apply two methods to locate, for each probing task, where the disambiguating information resides in the input. The first is a new perturbation method that “masks” various parts of context; the second is the classical method of Shapley values. The most intriguing finding that emerges is a strong tendency for the preceding context to hold more information relevant to the prediction than the following context.

papers.title: The Grammar-Learning Trajectories of Neural Language Models
papers.research_question: Do neural language models acquire linguistic phenomena in a consistent order during training, and what do their learning trajectories reveal about inductive biases?
papers.core_contribution: Neural language models acquire grammatical phenomena in a consistent order across different initializations, architectures, and training data, suggesting a shared inductive bias, and their learning trajectory is approximately one-dimensional.
papers.conclusion: NLMs exhibit consistent learning trajectories, providing a valuable perspective for studying their inductive biases and linguistic representations, complementary to analyzing final model states.
papers.key_findings:
NLMs with different random initializations learn grammatical phenomena in a highly correlated order.
Different architectures (GPT2, TransformerXL) show similar learning trajectories when aligned by overall performance.
The choice of training data affects the learning trajectory but does not override the shared order; correlation increases with training.
The learning trajectory is essentially one-dimensional: models with similar overall performance have similar grammatical knowledge.
Early learning stages rely on local cues (e.g., bag-of-words), while later stages incorporate more context and structural information.
future_direction: Investigate the impact of additional factors, architectures, and learning phases that appear later in training.
papers.abstract: The learning trajectories of linguistic phenomena in humans provide insight into linguistic representation, beyond what can be gleaned from inspecting the behavior of an adult speaker. To apply a similar approach to analyze neural language models (NLM), it is first necessary to establish that different models are similar enough in the generalizations they make. In this paper, we show that NLMs with different initialization, architecture, and training data acquire linguistic phenomena in a similar order, despite their different end performance. These findings suggest that there is some mutual inductive bias that underlies these models' learning of linguistic phenomena. Taking inspiration from psycholinguistics, we argue that studying this inductive bias is an opportunity to study the linguistic representation implicit in NLMs. Leveraging these findings, we compare the relative performance on different phenomena at varying learning stages with simpler reference models. Results suggest that NLMs exhibit consistent "developmental" stages. Moreover, we find the learning trajectory to be approximately one-dimensional: given an NLM with a certain overall performance, it is possible to predict what linguistic generalizations it has already acquired. Initial analysis of these stages presents phenomena clusters (notably morphological ones), whose performance progresses in unison, suggesting a potential link between the generalizations behind them.

papers.title: Morph Call: Probing Morphosyntactic Content of Multilingual Transformers
papers.research_question: What morphosyntactic knowledge do multilingual transformer models encode, and how does fine-tuning for POS-tagging affect this knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Morph Call, a suite of 46 probing tasks for four languages, and uses multiple introspection methods to analyze morphosyntactic knowledge in multilingual transformers, finding that fine-tuning for POS-tagging can both improve and decrease probing performance and change knowledge distribution.
papers.conclusion: The paper presents Morph Call, a probing suite for morphosyntactic content, and finds that knowledge distribution depends on language morphology (with English differing from more morphologically rich languages) and that fine-tuning for POS-tagging can affect the models in multiple ways.
papers.key_findings:
Multilingual transformers learn morphosyntactic content in a similar manner across languages, with properties distributed across middle-to-higher layers.
Masked token tasks are more challenging and show unstable performance across layers, with properties best inferred at middle-to-higher layers.
Models are sensitive to syntactic and inflectional perturbations, with syntactic perturbations better solved than inflectional ones.
Distilled models (D-BERT, MiniLM) mimic their teachers' behavior on some tasks but may show uncertain behavior on others.
Fine-tuning for POS-tagging affects model knowledge in various ways: it can improve or decrease probing performance, change the localization of information, and alter the number of neurons required for a property.
future_direction: Analyze the correlation between the number of neurons and probe performance after fine-tuning.
Explore fine-tuning for morphosyntactic analysis over UniMorph.
Test the hypothesis on a more diverse set of morphologically contrasting languages.
papers.abstract: The outstanding performance of transformerbased language models on a great variety of NLP and NLU tasks has stimulated interest in exploring their inner workings. Recent research has focused primarily on higherlevel and complex linguistic phenomena such as syntax, semantics, world knowledge, and common sense. The majority of the studies are anglocentric, and little remains known regarding other languages, precisely their morphosyntactic properties. To this end, our work presents Morph Call, a suite of 46 probing tasks for four Indo-European languages of different morphology: English, French, German and Russian. We propose a new type of probing task based on the detection of guided sentence perturbations. We use a combination of neuron-, layer-and representation-level introspection techniques to analyze the morphosyntactic content of four multilingual transformers, including their less explored distilled versions. Besides, we examine how fine-tuning for POS-tagging affects the model knowledge. The results show that fine-tuning can improve and decrease the probing performance and change how morphosyntactic knowledge is distributed across the model. The code and data are publicly available, and we hope to fill the gaps in the less studied aspect of transformers.

papers.title: Accurate Word Alignment Induction from Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: Do attention weights in Transformer models capture accurate word alignments, and how can word alignments be better induced from neural machine translation models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that Transformer attention weights can capture accurate word alignments if the correct decoding step and layer are chosen, and introduces two novel methods (SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET) that induce alignments at the step when the target token is the decoder input, significantly improving alignment accuracy.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET effectively induce word alignments from Transformer models, with SHIFT-AET achieving state-of-the-art performance without compromising translation quality.
papers.key_findings:
SHIFT-ATT, a pure interpretation method, reduces AER by 7.0-10.2 points over the NAIVE-ATT baseline and 5.5-7.9 points over FAST-ALIGN on three datasets.
SHIFT-AET, which adds and trains an alignment module supervised by SHIFT-ATT alignments, outperforms the statistical aligner GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.
A proposed layer selection criterion, based on agreement between source-to-target and target-to-source model alignments, effectively identifies the best layer for alignment induction.
Both SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET improve performance on the downstream task of dictionary-guided decoding compared to the NAIVE-ATT baseline.
Probing experiments show decoder hidden states at lower layers are more relevant to the input token than the output token, validating the shift in alignment step.
future_direction: Extend the study to more downstream tasks and systems.
papers.abstract: Despite its original goal to jointly learn to align and translate, prior researches suggest that Transformer captures poor word alignments through its attention mechanism. In this paper, we show that attention weights DO capture accurate word alignments and propose two novel word alignment induction methods SHIFT-ATT and SHIFT-AET. The main idea is to induce alignments at the step when the to-be-aligned target token is the decoder input rather than the decoder output as in previous work. SHIFT-ATT is an interpretation method that induces alignments from the attention weights of Transformer and does not require parameter update or architecture change. SHIFT-AET extracts alignments from an additional alignment module which is tightly integrated into Transformer and trained in isolation with supervision from symmetrized SHIFT-ATT alignments. Experiments on three publicly available datasets demonstrate that both methods perform better than their corresponding neural baselines and SHIFT-AET significantly outperforms GIZA++ by 1.4-4.8 AER points.

papers.title: Scaling Laws and Interpretability of Learning from Repeated Data
papers.research_question: What are the effects of repeated data on language model training, and how does it mechanistically affect model components like induction heads?
papers.core_contribution: Repeated data causes a double-descent phenomenon in language models, leading to severe performance degradation that is mechanistically linked to disproportionate damage to induction heads and copying mechanisms, shifting the model from generalization to memorization.
papers.conclusion: Small fractions of repeated data, if repeated at a specific frequency, can cause surprisingly severe performance degradation in language models, and this degradation is associated with disproportionate damage to internal mechanisms like induction heads that support generalization.
papers.key_findings:
Repeated data induces a strong double-descent phenomenon, with a predictable range of repetition frequency causing severe performance degradation.
A small fraction of repeated data (e.g., 0.1% repeated 100 times) can degrade an 800M parameter model's performance to that of a 400M parameter model.
Repeated data disproportionately damages copying ability and induction heads, which are internal structures associated with generalization.
The damage to induction heads provides a mechanistic explanation for the shift from generalization to memorization.
The double-descent phenomenon and associated performance degradation are also observed when training on Python code data.
papers.abstract: Recent large language models have been trained on vast datasets, but also often on repeated data, either intentionally for the purpose of upweighting higher quality data, or unintentionally because data deduplication is not perfect and the model is exposed to repeated data at the sentence, paragraph, or document level. Some works have reported substantial negative performance effects of this repeated data. In this paper we attempt to study repeated data systematically and to understand its effects mechanistically. To do this, we train a family of models where most of the data is unique but a small fraction of it is repeated many times. We find a strong double descent phenomenon, in which repeated data can lead test loss to increase midway through training. A predictable range of repetition frequency leads to surprisingly severe degradation in performance. For instance, performance of an 800M parameter model can be degraded to that of a 2x smaller model (400M params) by repeating 0.1% of the data 100 times, despite the other 90% of the training tokens remaining unique. We suspect there is a range in the middle where the data can be memorized and doing so consumes a large fraction of the model's capacity, and this may be where the peak of degradation occurs. Finally, we connect these observations to recent mechanistic interpretability work - attempting to reverse engineer the detailed computations performed by the model - by showing that data repetition disproportionately damages copying and internal structures associated with generalization, such as induction heads, providing a possible mechanism for the shift from generalization to memorization. Taken together, these results provide a hypothesis for why repeating a relatively small fraction of data in large language models could lead to disproportionately large harms to performance.

papers.title: Studying the Inductive Biases of RNNs with Synthetic Variations of Natural Languages
papers.research_question: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a methodology for generating synthetic languages by parametrically modifying parsed corpora to study the inductive biases of RNNs, and uses it to show that RNNs have a recency bias, that polypersonal agreement improves performance, and that overt case marking facilitates agreement prediction.
papers.conclusion: The proposed methodology is effective for studying grammatical inductive biases of RNNs, and the findings reveal that RNNs exhibit a recency bias, benefit from multitask agreement prediction, and are aided by case marking.
papers.key_findings:
Performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (SVO) than in subject-object-verb order (SOV), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias.
Predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across tasks.
Overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.
papers.limitation:
The reordering manipulation is limited to core elements (subjects, objects, and verbs) and does not consider word order inside other types of phrases.
The synthetic languages are simpler than natural languages because word order is completely fixed or fully flexible, while natural languages often have more complex and varied word order patterns.
future_direction: Exploring whether consistent reordering across phrase categories (head directionality parameter) improves model performance.
Conducting human experiments based on the agreement prediction task to compare human and RNN learning.
papers.abstract: How do typological properties such as word order and morphological case marking affect the ability of neural sequence models to acquire the syntax of a language? Cross-linguistic comparisons of RNNs' syntactic performance (e.g., on subject-verb agreement prediction) are complicated by the fact that any two languages differ in multiple typological properties, as well as by differences in training corpus. We propose a paradigm that addresses these issues: we create synthetic versions of English, which differ from English in one or more typological parameters, and generate corpora for those languages based on a parsed English corpus. We report a series of experiments in which RNNs were trained to predict agreement features for verbs in each of those synthetic languages. Among other findings, (1) performance was higher in subject-verb-object order (as in English) than in subject-object-verb order (as in Japanese), suggesting that RNNs have a recency bias; (2) predicting agreement with both subject and object (polypersonal agreement) improves over predicting each separately, suggesting that underlying syntactic knowledge transfers across the two tasks; and (3) overt morphological case makes agreement prediction significantly easier, regardless of word order.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Circuit Component Reuse Across Tasks in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and whether insights from circuit analysis generalize across tasks.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that circuit components are reused across different tasks in transformer language models, and that interventions based on one circuit can improve performance on another task, providing evidence for task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.conclusion: Circuit components are reused across tasks, providing evidence that large language models' behavior can be explained in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks.
papers.key_findings:
The IOI circuit reproduces on GPT2-Medium, with minor differences such as the negative mover head attending only to the S2 token.
The Colored Objects circuit shares about 78% of the important attention heads with the IOI circuit, indicating high component reuse.
Interventions on inhibition heads and the negative mover head can boost accuracy on the Colored Objects task from 49.6% to 93.7%.
The inhibition-mover head subcircuit behaves invariantly across tasks, as predicted by the IOI circuit.
The negative mover head in GPT2-Medium exhibits more sophisticated behavior than in GPT2-Small, directly demoting the subject token.
papers.limitation:
Quantifying circuit overlap is complex and not fully addressed in this paper.
The generality of the circuit beyond the studied tasks is not confirmed.
future_direction: Understanding how commonly the mover circuit is used by GPT2 in other tasks.
Developing methods for quantifying circuit overlap.
Studying circuit reuse in larger models.
papers.abstract: Recent work in mechanistic interpretability has shown that behaviors in language models can be successfully reverse-engineered through circuit analysis. A common criticism, however, is that each circuit is task-specific, and thus such analysis cannot contribute to understanding the models at a higher level. In this work, we present evidence that insights (both low-level findings about specific heads and higher-level findings about general algorithms) can indeed generalize across tasks. Specifically, we study the circuit discovered in Wang et al. (2022) for the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task and 1.) show that it reproduces on a larger GPT2 model, and 2.) that it is mostly reused to solve a seemingly different task: Colored Objects (Ippolito & Callison-Burch, 2023). We provide evidence that the process underlying both tasks is functionally very similar, and contains about a 78% overlap in in-circuit attention heads. We further present a proof-of-concept intervention experiment, in which we adjust four attention heads in middle layers in order to 'repair' the Colored Objects circuit and make it behave like the IOI circuit. In doing so, we boost accuracy from 49.6% to 93.7% on the Colored Objects task and explain most sources of error. The intervention affects downstream attention heads in specific ways predicted by their interactions in the IOI circuit, indicating that this subcircuit behavior is invariant to the different task inputs. Overall, our results provide evidence that it may yet be possible to explain large language models' behavior in terms of a relatively small number of interpretable task-general algorithmic building blocks and computational components.

papers.title: Large Language Models are In-Context Semantic Reasoners rather than Symbolic Reasoners
papers.research_question: Are LLMs good in-context reasoners without semantics?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that semantics are vital for LLMs' in-context reasoning; they perform well when semantics align with commonsense but struggle with symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning, relying on superficial semantic connections rather than formal symbolic reasoning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs rely heavily on learned semantics for in-context reasoning, creating strong token connections that compose a superficial logical chain, rather than performing formal symbolic reasoning like humans.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs perform significantly better on reasoning tasks when semantics are consistent with commonsense compared to when semantics are decoupled (symbolic setting).
LLMs struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge.
Semantic knowledge is easier for LLMs to memorize than symbolic knowledge, but updating semantic knowledge has a higher forgetting ratio due to stronger correlations.
LLMs' reasoning performance is inferior to logic-based symbolic methods across all tested reasoning tasks (deduction, induction, abduction).
The length of the in-context information impacts reasoning performance, with shorter contexts leading to better results.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to specific datasets (Symbolic Tree, ProofWriter) and models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, LLaMA-7B).
Long-context reasoning is challenging for LLMs, as they struggle to select relevant information from excessively long prompts.
future_direction: Combining LLMs with non-parametric knowledge bases (e.g., graph databases) for more efficient and accurate knowledge updating and reasoning.
Further research on neural-symbolic AI systems to leverage the strengths of both neural and symbolic approaches.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of LLMs to better understand how they utilize semantics for reasoning.
papers.abstract: The emergent few-shot reasoning capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) have excited the natural language and machine learning community over recent years. Despite of numerous successful applications, the underlying mechanism of such in-context capabilities still remains unclear. In this work, we hypothesize that the learned \textit{semantics} of language tokens do the most heavy lifting during the reasoning process. Different from human's symbolic reasoning process, the semantic representations of LLMs could create strong connections among tokens, thus composing a superficial logical chain. To test our hypothesis, we decouple semantics from the language reasoning process and evaluate three kinds of reasoning abilities, i.e., deduction, induction and abduction. Our findings reveal that semantics play a vital role in LLMs' in-context reasoning -- LLMs perform significantly better when semantics are consistent with commonsense but struggle to solve symbolic or counter-commonsense reasoning tasks by leveraging in-context new knowledge. The surprising observations question whether modern LLMs have mastered the inductive, deductive and abductive reasoning abilities as in human intelligence, and motivate research on unveiling the magic existing within the black-box LLMs. On the whole, our analysis provides a novel perspective on the role of semantics in developing and evaluating language models' reasoning abilities. Code is available at {\url{https://github.com/XiaojuanTang/ICSR}}.

papers.title: Language Mixing in Reasoning Language Models: Patterns, Impact, and Internal Causes
papers.research_question: What are the patterns, performance impact, and internal causes of language mixing (reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt) in Reasoning Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of language mixing in Reasoning Language Models, showing it reflects latent internal processing preferences (a bias towards Latin and Han scripts) and that controlling the reasoning script via constrained decoding can significantly improve multilingual reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: Language mixing in RLMs is a systematic behavior tied to the models' internal language preferences; controlling the reasoning script based on these preferences offers a practical way to optimize multilingual reasoning performance and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Language mixing is most prevalent when the input language is neither English nor Chinese, suggesting these serve as internal pivot languages.
The degree of language mixing increases with task difficulty and is more pronounced in STEM subjects.
Distillation amplifies language mixing compared to the base backbone models.
Forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy for non-Latin/Han-script input languages.
The script composition of reasoning traces closely mirrors that of the model's internal representations (analyzed via Logit Lens), indicating language mixing reflects latent processing preferences.
papers.limitation: Analysis focuses on valid reasoning traces that conclude with a final answer, excluding cases of endless reasoning.
future_direction: Controlling and adapting the reasoning language to build more robust, interpretable, and user-aligned RLMs.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models (RLMs) excel at complex tasks by leveraging a chain-of-thought process to generate structured intermediate steps. However, language mixing, i.e., reasoning steps containing tokens from languages other than the prompt, has been observed in their outputs and shown to affect performance, though its impact remains debated. We present the first systematic study of language mixing in RLMs, examining its patterns, impact, and internal causes across 15 languages, 7 task difficulty levels, and 18 subject areas, and show how all three factors influence language mixing. Moreover, we demonstrate that the choice of reasoning language significantly affects performance: forcing models to reason in Latin or Han scripts via constrained decoding notably improves accuracy. Finally, we show that the script composition of reasoning traces closely aligns with that of the model's internal representations, indicating that language mixing reflects latent processing preferences in RLMs. Our findings provide actionable insights for optimizing multilingual reasoning and open new directions for controlling reasoning languages to build more interpretable and adaptable RLMs.

papers.title: On the Linguistic Representational Power of Neural Machine Translation Models
papers.research_question: How do neural machine translation models capture linguistic information (morphology, syntax, semantics) in their representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that neural machine translation models learn non-trivial linguistic information in their representations, with a hierarchical organization: lower layers capture local, low-level properties (morphology) and higher layers capture global, high-level properties (syntax, semantics).
papers.conclusion: Deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without direct supervision, learn a substantial amount of linguistic information, and the representations are organized in a hierarchical manner.
papers.key_findings:
Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model.
Lexical semantics and non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model.
Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units.
Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.
The target language impacts the kind of information learned by the MT system, with translation into morphologically-poorer languages leading to better source-side word representations.
papers.abstract: Despite the recent success of deep neural networks in natural language processing and other spheres of artificial intelligence, their interpretability remains a challenge. We analyze the representations learned by neural machine translation (NMT) models at various levels of granularity and evaluate their quality through relevant extrinsic properties. In particular, we seek answers to the following questions: (i) How accurately is word structure captured within the learned representations, which is an important aspect in translating morphologically rich languages? (ii) Do the representations capture long-range dependencies, and effectively handle syntactically divergent languages? (iii) Do the representations capture lexical semantics? We conduct a thorough investigation along several parameters: (i) Which layers in the architecture capture each of these linguistic phenomena; (ii) How does the choice of translation unit (word, character, or subword unit) impact the linguistic properties captured by the underlying representations? (iii) Do the encoder and decoder learn differently and independently? (iv) Do the representations learned by multilingual NMT models capture the same amount of linguistic information as their bilingual counterparts? Our data-driven, quantitative evaluation illuminates important aspects in NMT models and their ability to capture various linguistic phenomena. We show that deep NMT models trained in an end-to-end fashion, without being provided any direct supervision during the training process, learn a non-trivial amount of linguistic information. Notable findings include the following observations: (i) Word morphology and part-of-speech information are captured at the lower layers of the model; (ii) In contrast, lexical semantics or non-local syntactic and semantic dependencies are better represented at the higher layers of the model; (iii) Representations learned using characters are more informed about word-morphology compared to those learned using subword units; and (iv) Representations learned by multilingual models are richer compared to bilingual models.

papers.title: Shadow of the (Hierarchical) Tree: Reconciling Symbolic and Predictive Components of the Neural Code for Syntax
papers.research_question: How can symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks be integrated to account for both hierarchical (vertical) and linear/predictive (horizontal) aspects of natural language syntax?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a hybrid neurosymbolic model that reconciles symbolic hierarchical syntax and connectionist linear/predictive processes via oscillatory phase codes, specifically extending the ROSE architecture.
papers.conclusion: A hybrid neurosymbolic approach, using oscillatory phase codes, can reconcile symbolic and predictive components of syntax, providing a path forward for cognitive neuroscience and language modeling.
papers.key_findings:
The ROSE architecture provides a symbolic account of hierarchical syntax via oscillatory mechanisms like phase-amplitude coupling.
Horizontal syntactic information (linear, statistical) can be integrated via predictive coding and statistical inference at lower levels of ROSE.
Oscillatory phase codes (e.g., traveling waves modulating high-frequency spiking) provide a feasible interface between symbolic and statistical representations.
Large language models (LLMs) are more competent at modeling horizontal syntactic information than vertical hierarchical syntax, indicating a limitation in their compositional reasoning.
A mathematical model demonstrates how frontotemporal traveling waves can dynamically modulate high-frequency spiking activity to integrate symbolic and statistical information for morphosyntax.
future_direction: Integrating associationist and predictive neural mechanisms into the existing ROSE architecture.
Mathematical formalization of the ROSE architecture and its hybrid extensions.
Testing the proposed hybrid neurosymbolic model with empirical neural data.
papers.abstract: Natural language syntax can serve as a major test for how to integrate two infamously distinct frameworks: symbolic representations and connectionist neural networks. Building on a recent neurocomputational architecture for syntax (ROSE), I discuss the prospects of reconciling the neural code for hierarchical 'vertical' syntax with linear and predictive 'horizontal' processes via a hybrid neurosymbolic model. I argue that the former can be accounted for via the higher levels of ROSE in terms of vertical phrase structure representations, while the latter can explain horizontal forms of linguistic information via the tuning of the lower levels to statistical and perceptual inferences. One prediction of this is that artificial language models will contribute to the cognitive neuroscience of horizontal morphosyntax, but much less so to hierarchically compositional structures. I claim that this perspective helps resolve many current tensions in the literature. Options for integrating these two neural codes are discussed, with particular emphasis on how predictive coding mechanisms can serve as interfaces between symbolic oscillatory phase codes and population codes for the statistics of linearized aspects of syntax. Lastly, I provide a neurosymbolic mathematical model for how to inject symbolic representations into a neural regime encoding lexico-semantic statistical features.

papers.title: Reason to Rote: Rethinking Memorization in Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do language models memorize label noise, and why does such memorization not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Memorization of noisy labels in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, with memories stored via distributed encoding and outlier heuristics in neurons.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that memorization of label noise builds on existing reasoning mechanisms, using distributed encoding and outlier heuristics, explaining the phenomenon of benign memorization.
papers.key_findings:
Models first learn to generalize on noisy training instances (predicting correct labels) before memorizing the noisy labels.
Even when producing memorized noisy labels, models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs corresponding to the correct labels.
Memorization and generalization circuits substantially overlap, indicating memorization builds on existing generalization mechanisms.
Memorization uses distributed encoding across multiple input tokens and intermediate results rather than a simple lookup.
In the FDA task, memorization occurs via 'outlier heuristics' where higher-layer MLP neurons slightly shift their activation patterns to fit noisy labels.
papers.limitation:
Focus on relatively small language models; larger models might exhibit different behaviors.
Models trained from scratch, so influence of pretraining data is not considered.
Examination of implicit reasoning without explicit solution steps; not studying models with explicit chain-of-thought.
future_direction: Study memorization in larger models
Investigate effect of pretraining on memorization and reasoning
Study memorization in models with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.abstract: Large language models readily memorize arbitrary training instances, such as label noise, yet they perform strikingly well on reasoning tasks. In this work, we investigate how language models memorize label noise, and why such memorization in many cases does not heavily affect generalizable reasoning capabilities. Using two controllable synthetic reasoning datasets with noisy labels, four-digit addition (FDA) and two-hop relational reasoning (THR), we discover a reliance of memorization on generalizable reasoning mechanisms: models continue to compute intermediate reasoning outputs even when retrieving memorized noisy labels, and intervening reasoning adversely affects memorization. We further show that memorization operates through distributed encoding, i.e., aggregating various inputs and intermediate results, rather than building a look-up mechanism from inputs to noisy labels. Moreover, our FDA case study reveals memorization occurs via outlier heuristics, where existing neuron activation patterns are slightly shifted to fit noisy labels. Together, our findings suggest that memorization of label noise in language models builds on, rather than overrides, the underlying reasoning mechanisms, shedding lights on the intriguing phenomenon of benign memorization.

papers.title: In-Context Language Learning: Architectures and Algorithms
papers.research_question: Which model classes can perform in-context language learning (ICLL), what algorithmic solutions do they implement, and how can architectural changes improve ICLL?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces in-context language learning (ICLL) as a model problem for studying ICL, shows Transformers outperform other models by implementing n-gram heads, and demonstrates that adding n-gram heads improves ICLL and natural language modeling.
papers.conclusion: ICLL is a useful model problem for understanding ICL, and n-gram heads are a key mechanism in Transformers for ICLL that can be used to improve other models.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers significantly outperform recurrent and convolutional models on ICLL tasks.
Transformers develop specialized n-gram heads (higher-order induction heads) to compute in-context n-gram statistics.
Probing shows that Transformers better encode n-gram counts in hidden states compared to other models.
Hard-wiring n-gram heads into other models (RNNs, convolutional) improves their ICLL performance.
Adding n-gram heads also improves natural language modeling perplexity.
papers.limitation: Many aspects of ICLL, even with regular languages, remain to be understood (e.g. learning dynamics and out-of-distribution generalization).
future_direction: Extend ICLL to more expressive languages (context-free or context-sensitive)
Extend experiments to larger models trained with more tokens
papers.abstract: Large-scale neural language models exhibit a remarkable capacity for in-context learning (ICL): they can infer novel functions from datasets provided as input. Most of our current understanding of when and how ICL arises comes from LMs trained on extremely simple learning problems like linear regression and associative recall. There remains a significant gap between these model problems and the "real" ICL exhibited by LMs trained on large text corpora, which involves not just retrieval and function approximation but free-form generation of language and other structured outputs. In this paper, we study ICL through the lens of a new family of model problems we term in context language learning (ICLL). In ICLL, LMs are presented with a set of strings from a formal language, and must generate additional strings from the same language. We focus on in-context learning of regular languages generated by random finite automata. We evaluate a diverse set of neural sequence models (including several RNNs, Transformers, and state-space model variants) on regular ICLL tasks, aiming to answer three questions: (1) Which model classes are empirically capable of ICLL? (2) What algorithmic solutions do successful models implement to perform ICLL? (3) What architectural changes can improve ICLL in less performant models? We first show that Transformers significantly outperform neural sequence models with recurrent or convolutional representations on ICLL tasks. Next, we provide evidence that their ability to do so relies on specialized "n-gram heads" (higher-order variants of induction heads) that compute input-conditional next-token distributions. Finally, we show that hard-wiring these heads into neural models improves performance not just on ICLL, but natural language modeling -- improving the perplexity of 340M-parameter models by up to 1.14 points (6.7%) on the SlimPajama dataset.

papers.title: Language Embeddings Sometimes Contain Typological Generalizations
papers.research_question: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? Which typological features can be discovered when the system is not told what to look for?
papers.core_contribution: This paper finds that neural models can sometimes learn typological generalizations in their language representations, but less readily than suggested by prior work, and that careful evaluation is essential to avoid false positives. It also releases several resources for 1295 languages.
papers.conclusion: Neural models can discover typological generalizations, but they do so less readily than suggested by previous research, and careful evaluation is necessary to confirm such discoveries.
papers.key_findings:
Some generalizations in learned language representations are surprisingly close to traditional typological features, but most models (including those from previous work) do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations.
Careful attention to evaluation details, such as controlling for genealogical and areal correlations, is essential to avoid false positives.
The word-level language model (WordLM) captures word order features and some morphological features, while many other models (including MTVec, MTCell, and Ö&T) show little evidence of encoding typological features when evaluated with their method.
Lexical baselines (ASJP and Lexical similarity vectors) do not encode structural features, as expected, and can serve as a baseline for evaluation.
papers.limitation: The study only tries to connect neural language representations with known features from the typological literature, not with potentially novel generalizations.
future_direction: Investigating whether models make typological generalizations that human linguists have not previously made.
papers.abstract: To what extent can neural network models learn generalizations about language structure, and how do we find out what they have learned? We explore these questions by training neural models for a range of natural language processing tasks on a massively multilingual dataset of Bible translations in 1295 languages. The learned language representations are then compared to existing typological databases as well as to a novel set of quantitative syntactic and morphological features obtained through annotation projection. We conclude that some generalizations are surprisingly close to traditional features from linguistic typology, but that most of our models, as well as those of previous work, do not appear to have made linguistically meaningful generalizations. Careful attention to details in the evaluation turns out to be essential to avoid false positives. Furthermore, to encourage continued work in this field, we release several resources covering most or all of the languages in our data: (i) multiple sets of language representations, (ii) multilingual word embeddings, (iii) projected and predicted syntactic and morphological features, (iv) software to provide linguistically sound evaluations of language representations.

papers.title: TRACE for Tracking the Emergence of Semantic Representations in Transformers
papers.research_question: What geometric and statistical signals accompany the transition from memorisation to abstraction in sentence-level representations? When do syntactic and semantic categories emerge in transformer representations over training? What mechanisms and training dynamics trigger these phase transitions, and how do architectural and optimisation factors influence their onset?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces TRACE, a diagnostic framework combining geometric, informational, and linguistic signals to detect phase transitions in Transformer-based LMs, and ABSynth, a synthetic data generator. Shows that phase transitions align with curvature collapse and dimension stabilization, and that abstraction patterns persist across architectural variants.
papers.conclusion: TRACE provides a unified framework for tracking abstraction emergence, revealing that phase transitions are marked by coordinated geometric, informational, and linguistic shifts. This understanding can inform more efficient training and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Phase transitions align with clear intersections between curvature collapse and dimension stabilisation.
These geometric shifts coincide with emerging syntactic and semantic accuracy.
Abstraction patterns persist across architectural variants, with components like feedforward networks affecting optimisation stability rather than fundamentally altering trajectories.
Mutual information was found to be an unreliable diagnostic signal due to high volatility and lack of consistent alignment with phase transitions.
Probing reveals a two-phase developmental process where output behavior stabilizes early while internal representations continue restructuring.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic corpus does not fully capture the ambiguity and richness of natural language.
Probe-based diagnostics offer a static view of representation content and may not reflect dynamic computational mechanisms at inference time.
TRACE establishes strong correlations but does not establish causal relationships or quantify the relative contribution of each factor.
future_direction: Extending TRACE to natural language corpora and larger models.
Applying the framework to broader domains and pre-trained transformers.
Integrating TRACE with mechanistic interpretability tools to localise where and how abstraction-related circuits emerge.
papers.abstract: Modern transformer models exhibit phase transitions during training, distinct shifts from memorisation to abstraction, but the mechanisms underlying these transitions remain poorly understood. Prior work has often focused on endpoint representations or isolated signals like curvature or mutual information, typically in symbolic or arithmetic domains, overlooking the emergence of linguistic structure. We introduce TRACE (Tracking Representation Abstraction and Compositional Emergence), a diagnostic framework combining geometric, informational, and linguistic signals to detect phase transitions in Transformer-based LMs. TRACE leverages a frame-semantic data generation method, ABSynth, that produces annotated synthetic corpora with controllable complexity, lexical distributions, and structural entropy, while being fully annotated with linguistic categories, enabling precise analysis of abstraction emergence. Experiments reveal that (i) phase transitions align with clear intersections between curvature collapse and dimension stabilisation; (ii) these geometric shifts coincide with emerging syntactic and semantic accuracy; (iii) abstraction patterns persist across architectural variants, with components like feedforward networks affecting optimisation stability rather than fundamentally altering trajectories. This work advances our understanding of how linguistic abstractions emerge in LMs, offering insights into model interpretability, training efficiency, and compositional generalisation that could inform more principled approaches to LM development.

papers.title: Do RNN States Encode Abstract Phonological Processes?
papers.research_question: Do RNN states encode abstract phonological processes? Specifically, does a sequence-to-sequence model learn a generalized representation of Finnish consonant gradation, or does it memorize each process separately?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that RNN encoder-decoder models can encode abstract phonological processes like Finnish consonant gradation in a handful of hidden state dimensions, and that scaling these activations can control whether gradation occurs and its direction.
papers.conclusion: The paper provides evidence that RNNs can learn a generalized representation of phonological alternations, and that these representations can be manipulated to control model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
The models often encode 17 different consonant gradation processes in a few encoder hidden state dimensions, indicating a generalized representation.
Scaling the activations in these identified dimensions can 'switch off' gradation, causing the model to generate non-gradating forms.
The direction of gradation (direct/weakening vs. inverse/strengthening) can be encoded as positive or negative activation in certain dimensions.
The learned representation can generalize across different types of gradation (quantitative and qualitative) and across the consonants p, t, and k.
This behavior is not universal; some models fail to generalize and instead use distinct dimensions for each stop.
papers.limitation:
The generalized representation of gradation is not universal across all trained models; some models fail to generalize and use distinct dimensions for each stop.
The investigation into generalization to voiced stops (like b and g) was not conclusive and is left for future work.
future_direction: A detailed study of whether the model generalizes gradation from voiceless stops to their voiced counterparts (like b and g) in loanwords.
papers.abstract: Sequence-to-sequence models have delivered impressive results in word formation tasks such as morphological inflection, often learning to model subtle morphophonological details with limited training data. Despite the performance, the opacity of neural models makes it difficult to determine whether complex generalizations are learned, or whether a kind of separate rote memorization of each morphophonological process takes place. To investigate whether complex alternations are simply memorized or whether there is some level of generalization across related sound changes in a sequence-to-sequence model, we perform several experiments on Finnish consonant gradation -- a complex set of sound changes triggered in some words by certain suffixes. We find that our models often -- though not always -- encode 17 different consonant gradation processes in a handful of dimensions in the RNN. We also show that by scaling the activations in these dimensions we can control whether consonant gradation occurs and the direction of the gradation.

papers.title: LINSPECTOR: Multilingual Probing Tasks for Word Representations
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate word representation models in a multilingual setting to understand what linguistic features they capture and how this correlates with downstream task performance?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces LINSPECTOR, a set of multilingual probing tasks and an evaluation suite for word representations, and shows that probing task performance correlates with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that the introduced probing tasks and the LINSPECTOR framework are effective for evaluating word representations in multiple languages and that they correlate with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
papers.key_findings:
Probing tasks can be used to evaluate word embeddings in multiple languages and show significant positive correlation with downstream task performance, especially for morphologically rich languages.
All embedding models achieved their lowest score for CharacterBin, a task that requires predicting the number of characters.
D-ELMo achieves the highest scores in probing for all language-test pairs, generally followed by fastText and GloVe-BPE.
Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
The probing tasks can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting.
papers.limitation: Token-level tasks may be influenced by domain and majority class biases, while type-level tasks may suffer from lack of lexical diversity and high ambiguity ratios.
future_direction: Extend probing tasks to more languages and include more linguistic phenomena.
Investigate the use of probing tasks for model selection and hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Despite an ever-growing number of word representation models introduced for a large number of languages, there is a lack of a standardized technique to provide insights into what is captured by these models. Such insights would help the community to get an estimate of the downstream task performance, as well as to design more informed neural architectures, while avoiding extensive experimentation that requires substantial computational resources not all researchers have access to. A recent development in NLP is to use simple classification tasks, also called probing tasks, that test for a single linguistic feature such as part-of-speech. Existing studies mostly focus on exploring the linguistic information encoded by the continuous representations of English text. However, from a typological perspective the morphologically poor English is rather an outlier: The information encoded by the word order and function words in English is often stored on a subword, morphological level in other languages. To address this, we introduce 15 type-level probing tasks such as case marking, possession, word length, morphological tag count, and pseudoword identification for 24 languages. We present a reusable methodology for creation and evaluation of such tests in a multilingual setting, which is challenging because of a lack of resources, lower quality of tools, and differences among languages. We then present experiments on several diverse multilingual word embedding models, in which we relate the probing task performance for a diverse set of languages to a range of five classic NLP tasks: POS-tagging, dependency parsing, semantic role labeling, named entity recognition, and natural language inference. We find that a number of probing tests have significantly high positive correlation to the downstream tasks, especially for morphologically rich languages. We show that our tests can be used to explore word embeddings or black-box neural models for linguistic cues in a multilingual setting. We release the probing data sets and the evaluation suite LINSPECTOR with https://github.com/UKPLab/linspector .

papers.title: Large Language Models Share Representations of Latent Grammatical Concepts Across Typologically Diverse Languages
papers.research_question: In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphosyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages.
papers.core_contribution: Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.
papers.conclusion: Large language models share representations of morphosyntactic concepts across typologically diverse languages, suggesting that they develop cross-lingual abstractions, even when trained primarily on English.
papers.key_findings:
Representations of morphosyntactic concepts are shared across languages, with significant overlap in the top features encoding grammatical categories.
Probing classifiers crucially rely on multilingual features to predict morphosyntactic concepts; ablating multilingual features drops performance to near-chance.
Intervening on single multilingual features can change model behavior in machine translation tasks, demonstrating their causal role.
Interventions are selective, primarily affecting the targeted concept without interfering with other concepts.
Sparse autoencoder features are human-interpretable and activate on relevant grammatical concepts across languages.
papers.limitation:
Distinction between model understanding and generation; some features with high causal effect on probes do not necessarily affect generation.
Human biases in feature interpretation; human explanations of features may be biased and suboptimal.
Sparse autoencoders only recover linearly encoded features; non-linearly encoded concepts may not be captured.
papers.abstract: Human bilinguals often use similar brain regions to process multiple languages, depending on when they learned their second language and their proficiency. In large language models (LLMs), how are multiple languages learned and encoded? In this work, we explore the extent to which LLMs share representations of morphsyntactic concepts such as grammatical number, gender, and tense across languages. We train sparse autoencoders on Llama-3-8B and Aya-23-8B, and demonstrate that abstract grammatical concepts are often encoded in feature directions shared across many languages. We use causal interventions to verify the multilingual nature of these representations; specifically, we show that ablating only multilingual features decreases classifier performance to near-chance across languages. We then use these features to precisely modify model behavior in a machine translation task; this demonstrates both the generality and selectivity of these feature's roles in the network. Our findings suggest that even models trained predominantly on English data can develop robust, cross-lingual abstractions of morphosyntactic concepts.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Sentiment in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How is sentiment represented within Large Language Models (LLMs)? Specifically, is it represented linearly and what are the mechanisms involved?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs via a single direction in activation space, demonstrates its causal relevance through interventions, and discovers a 'summarization motif' where sentiment is aggregated at intermediate tokens like commas.
papers.conclusion: The work shows that sentiment is linearly represented and causally relevant in LLMs, identifies a summarization motif, and contributes to understanding internal feature representation, suggesting directions for future interpretability research.
papers.key_findings:
Sentiment is represented linearly in LLMs: a single direction in activation space captures sentiment across tasks and models.
This sentiment direction is causally relevant for sentiment tasks, as shown by activation patching and ablation experiments.
The sentiment direction generalizes across models and out-of-distribution datasets.
The model uses a circuit involving specific attention heads and neurons to process sentiment.
The summarization motif: sentiment information is aggregated at intermediate tokens without inherent valence (e.g., commas, periods), acting as information bottlenecks.
papers.limitation:
Analysis is primarily on decoder-only models, and may not generalize to other architectures.
Toy datasets are simple and may not capture full natural language complexity.
Causal interventions may not fully capture model dynamics on more complex tasks.
future_direction: Extend methods to other features beyond sentiment, such as toxicity or deception.
Investigate the summarization motif in other tasks and models.
Develop more robust methods for finding linear directions in larger models.
papers.abstract: Sentiment is a pervasive feature in natural language text, yet it is an open question how sentiment is represented within Large Language Models (LLMs). In this study, we reveal that across a range of models, sentiment is represented linearly: a single direction in activation space mostly captures the feature across a range of tasks with one extreme for positive and the other for negative. Through causal interventions, we isolate this direction and show it is causally relevant in both toy tasks and real world datasets such as Stanford Sentiment Treebank. Through this case study we model a thorough investigation of what a single direction means on a broad data distribution. We further uncover the mechanisms that involve this direction, highlighting the roles of a small subset of attention heads and neurons. Finally, we discover a phenomenon which we term the summarization motif: sentiment is not solely represented on emotionally charged words, but is additionally summarized at intermediate positions without inherent sentiment, such as punctuation and names. We show that in Stanford Sentiment Treebank zero-shot classification, 76% of above-chance classification accuracy is lost when ablating the sentiment direction, nearly half of which (36%) is due to ablating the summarized sentiment direction exclusively at comma positions.

papers.title: Decoding Probing: Revealing Internal Linguistic Structures in Neural Language Models using Minimal Pairs
papers.research_question: How do neural language models capture linguistic information internally, specifically using minimal pairs to probe grammaticality across layers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a novel 'decoding probing' method inspired by cognitive neuroscience to reveal internal linguistic structures in neural language models using minimal pairs, demonstrating that self-supervised models capture abstract linguistic features in intermediate layers with distinct patterns for syntax, morphology, and semantics.
papers.conclusion: Decoding probing bridges cognitive neuroscience and NLP, providing insights into hierarchical linguistic feature capture in LMs, with semantics-syntax interface and morphology being more challenging than syntax.
papers.key_findings:
Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn.
Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and distributed in later layers; more layers are required for complex sentences.
Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax.
For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns, with attention heads exhibiting similar tendencies but varied contributions.
papers.limitation: Focuses mainly on structure grammaticality with limited attention to conceptual capabilities.
future_direction: Apply decoding probe methods to reveal LM's ability to master concepts using the COMPS minimal pair dataset.
papers.abstract: Inspired by cognitive neuroscience studies, we introduce a novel `decoding probing' method that uses minimal pairs benchmark (BLiMP) to probe internal linguistic characteristics in neural language models layer by layer. By treating the language model as the `brain' and its representations as `neural activations', we decode grammaticality labels of minimal pairs from the intermediate layers' representations. This approach reveals: 1) Self-supervised language models capture abstract linguistic structures in intermediate layers that GloVe and RNN language models cannot learn. 2) Information about syntactic grammaticality is robustly captured through the first third layers of GPT-2 and also distributed in later layers. As sentence complexity increases, more layers are required for learning grammatical capabilities. 3) Morphological and semantics/syntax interface-related features are harder to capture than syntax. 4) For Transformer-based models, both embeddings and attentions capture grammatical features but show distinct patterns. Different attention heads exhibit similar tendencies toward various linguistic phenomena, but with varied contributions.

papers.title: Can Transformer be Too Compositional? Analysing Idiom Processing in Neural Machine Translation
papers.research_question: How does the Transformer-based neural machine translation model process idioms, and is the non-compositionality of idioms reflected in its mechanics?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer tends to translate idioms too compositionally, and when it produces non-literal translations, the encoder groups idiom parts more strongly as a single unit, with reduced interaction with context and reduced cross-attention on source tokens.
papers.conclusion: Transformer's tendency to process idioms compositionally contributes to literal translations, and techniques that encourage compositionality in NMT may be detrimental for non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.key_findings:
Figurative idioms receive more attention within the PIE in encoder self-attention compared to literal idioms.
Figurative idioms have reduced attention between the PIE and its context.
In cross-attention, figurative idioms lead to reduced attention on source-side PIE tokens and increased attention on the </s> token.
Hidden representations of figurative idioms change more across layers than those of literal idioms.
Intervening with INLP to remove linearly encoded features of figurativeness can change paraphrased translations to word-for-word, indicating a causal link.
papers.limitation:
Heuristic annotation method for translations has imperfect accuracy (75-89% for key categories).
Analysis is limited to seven European languages.
future_direction: Architectural changes to improve grouping of idioms as single units, e.g., training specific attention heads or penalizing overly compositional translations.
Evaluate the effect of compositionality-favouring techniques on non-compositional phenomena like idioms.
papers.abstract: Unlike literal expressions, idioms' meanings do not directly follow from their parts, posing a challenge for neural machine translation (NMT). NMT models are often unable to translate idioms accurately and over-generate compositional, literal translations. In this work, we investigate whether the non-compositionality of idioms is reflected in the mechanics of the dominant NMT model, Transformer, by analysing the hidden states and attention patterns for models with English as source language and one of seven European languages as target language.When Transformer emits a non-literal translation - i.e. identifies the expression as idiomatic - the encoder processes idioms more strongly as single lexical units compared to literal expressions. This manifests in idioms' parts being grouped through attention and in reduced interaction between idioms and their context.In the decoder's cross-attention, figurative inputs result in reduced attention on source-side tokens. These results suggest that Transformer's tendency to process idioms as compositional expressions contributes to literal translations of idioms.

papers.title: Uncovering mesa-optimization algorithms in Transformers
papers.research_question: How does in-context learning emerge in autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction? The paper investigates whether such training gives rise to a gradient-based optimization algorithm (mesa-optimizer) that adjusts the model as new inputs are revealed.
papers.core_contribution: Autoregressive Transformers trained on next-token prediction learn a gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithm that performs in-context learning, explaining the emergence of in-context learning and inspiring new Transformer layers.
papers.conclusion: In-context learning in autoregressive Transformers arises from mesa-optimization algorithms learned during training, which can be leveraged to design more efficient optimization-based layers.
papers.key_findings:
Early Transformer layers learn a token binding mechanism that aggregates consecutive observations into internal representations, enabling subsequent mesa-optimization.
Trained single-layer linear self-attention models implement one-step gradient descent on a least-squares objective, matching the theoretical construction.
Multi-layer linear self-attention models implement a preconditioned gradient descent algorithm that approximates the optimal least-squares solution.
The proposed mesa-layer, derived from optimization principles, performs recursive least squares and improves language modeling performance compared to standard linear attention.
Standard softmax Transformers trained on synthetic sequence tasks exhibit internal activation patterns consistent with mesa-optimization across layers.
papers.limitation: The language modeling results are not sufficient to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers; more reverse-engineering is needed.
future_direction: Studying the mesa-layer equipped with forgetting factors
More reverse-engineering work to confirm mesa-optimization in standard Transformers
Designing new optimization-based Transformer layers
papers.abstract: Transformers have become the dominant model in deep learning, but the reason for their superior performance is poorly understood. Here, we hypothesize that the strong performance of Transformers stems from an architectural bias towards mesa-optimization, a learned process running within the forward pass of a model consisting of the following two steps: (i) the construction of an internal learning objective, and (ii) its corresponding solution found through optimization. To test this hypothesis, we reverse-engineer a series of autoregressive Transformers trained on simple sequence modeling tasks, uncovering underlying gradient-based mesa-optimization algorithms driving the generation of predictions. Moreover, we show that the learned forward-pass optimization algorithm can be immediately repurposed to solve supervised few-shot tasks, suggesting that mesa-optimization might underlie the in-context learning capabilities of large language models. Finally, we propose a novel self-attention layer, the mesa-layer, that explicitly and efficiently solves optimization problems specified in context. We find that this layer can lead to improved performance in synthetic and preliminary language modeling experiments, adding weight to our hypothesis that mesa-optimization is an important operation hidden within the weights of trained Transformers.

papers.title: Diversity of Transformer Layers: One Aspect of Parameter Scaling Laws
papers.research_question: How do the internal layer dynamics (specifically the diversity of layer outputs) in Transformers relate to parameter scaling laws?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that diversity of predictions from each module in the Transformer residual stream is crucial for performance, and that adding layers improves performance only when layers are diverse, with diminishing returns that align with parameter scaling laws.
papers.conclusion: The diversity of predictions from each module on the residual stream is important for improving Transformer performance, and the effectiveness of adding layers diminishes as the number of layers increases, consistent with parameter scaling laws.
papers.key_findings:
Performance improves when individual layers make predictions close to the correct answer and remain mutually diverse.
Diversity becomes especially critical when individual layers' outputs are far from the ground truth.
Adding layers enhances performance only when those layers behave differently (are diverse).
The performance gains from increasing layers exhibit submodularity: marginal improvements diminish as additional layers increase, mirroring the logarithmic convergence predicted by parameter scaling laws.
Experiments on multiple semantic-understanding tasks with various LLMs empirically confirm these theoretical properties.
